name: Glutamine

card.summary: The most abundant amino acid in blood, sold as a muscle-recovery supplement; its clinical evidence lies in medicine, not physique.
card.note: A prescription L-glutamine powder is FDA-approved for sickle cell disease; no trials in the reference material test it for muscle gain.

quick.overview:
Glutamine is a conditionally essential amino acid that the body makes in large amounts, mostly in muscle. It is sold as a supplement, often to people who lift weights, with the idea that it supports recovery and muscle retention.

The documented clinical uses are medical. A prescription form was approved by the US FDA in 2017 for sickle cell disease, and it is used in some hospital nutrition settings, where evidence is described as low quality.
quick.mechanism: Glutamine is a protein building block, a nitrogen carrier between organs, and a fuel for gut-lining and immune cells. It is also used to make glutathione. Supplement marketing builds on these roles, but the reference sources reviewed here do not report trials showing muscle growth in healthy lifters.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes supplemental glutamine as considered safe in adults, with an observed safe level of 14 g/day in healthy adults, and notes adverse effects in people on home parenteral nutrition or with liver abnormalities. Side effects of the prescription form include constipation, nausea, headache and abdominal pain.

lead: Glutamine (Gln, Q) is an alpha-amino acid used in protein synthesis and the most abundant free amino acid in human blood. It is classed as non-essential but conditionally essential, because demand can exceed supply during stress such as illness or injury.[1][2] Roughly 90 percent of it is made in muscle tissue, and the intestines, kidneys, activated immune cells and many cancer cells use it heavily.[2]

In appearance-related communities it is sold as a supplement for muscle recovery and muscle preservation, and it appears in combination products marketed for body composition.[3] Its documented clinical uses are different: an oral L-glutamine powder was approved by the US FDA in 2017 for reducing complications of sickle cell disease, and glutamine has been studied in surgery, critical illness and gut disorders.[2][4]

Wikipedia's article does not discuss bodybuilding or athletic performance evidence, and the reference material reviewed for this entry contains no trial of glutamine supplementation for muscle gain in healthy people.[2]

paras: Glutamine serves as a protein building block, a nitrogen donor for purine synthesis, a carbon source that refills the citric acid cycle, and a precursor for glutathione, which helps maintain redox balance. It also carries ammonia non-toxically in blood, and kidney cells use it in acid-base regulation.[2][1]
It is synthesized from glutamate and ammonia by glutamine synthetase, mainly in muscle, liver and brain, and is obtained from the diet in protein-rich foods.[1]

In 2017 the US FDA approved L-glutamine oral powder (Endari) to reduce severe complications of sickle cell disease in people aged five and older. It also carries an orphan drug designation.[2] Glutamine is additionally sold as a medical food for patients a clinician judges to need more than diet and metabolism supply.[2]

Reviews of glutamine in critical illness and surgery are described by Wikipedia as based on low-quality evidence, with no firm conclusions; Cochrane-type reviews found insufficient evidence for Crohn's disease, and results for mucositis are mixed.[2]

In a 48-week randomized trial in sickle cell disease summarised by Wikipedia, treated patients had fewer pain-related hospital visits (median 3 versus 4), fewer hospitalizations (median 2 versus 3) and fewer hospital days (median 6.5 versus 11) than placebo; acute chest syndrome occurred in 8.6 percent versus 23.1 percent.[2]

Registered trials include a phase 2 study in diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (106 participants) and small studies of the prescription powder in diabetes, diverticulosis and thalassemia.[5][6] Some trials and meta-analyses report reduced markers of intestinal permeability after intense exercise or critical illness; results in chronic inflammatory conditions are inconsistent.[2] No trial of glutamine for muscle size or appearance outcomes in healthy people appears in the reference material reviewed.

Wikipedia reports that glutamine is considered safe in adults and preterm infants, with an observed safe level of 14 g/day for supplemental glutamine in healthy adults. Adverse effects have been described in people on home parenteral nutrition and in those with liver abnormalities, and supplementation may be harmful in some cancer types. Stopping after very high long-term intake may cause withdrawal effects.[2]
Common side effects of the prescription form are constipation, nausea, headache and abdominal pain.[2]

Glutamine is an ingredient in multi-component supplements. One US drug-label listing for an oral product containing glutamine alongside arginine pyroglutamate, ornithine alpha-ketoglutarate, Tribulus terrestris and other ingredients states that it temporarily supports the body in rebalancing human growth hormone output.[3]

timeline.event: US FDA approves L-glutamine oral powder (Endari) for sickle cell disease.[2]
